<reason>Both sides executed well, but Side A held the stronger end-to-end path. A's live route—the asymmetric incentive structure (conspicuous penalty for teaching contested material, near-zero penalty for quiet omission)—was never attacked on mechanism, only on measurability, and A's answer (CON's counter-examples are equally unmeasured; "harder to detect" ≠ "unknowable") blunted B's central burden attack. B's cleverest move, the "category collapse" (serious omission-harm converts into a content defect), was met with a genuinely decisive rejoinder in A's closing: the harm's form does not change its cause, and the motion ranks threats by cause—political fear produced the miseducation and simultaneously weakened the corrective capacity that would fix it. B's final reply ("inference is not instruction; a gap sits lightly") was thin against the reality that curated omissions do mislead. B also leaned on "documented damage" while offering only asserted examples, and both B rebuttals were clipped at the word limit, a minor execution cost. B's rhetoric and discipline were excellent, but A did more comparative work on substance.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The B4.3 "category collapse" versus A5.1 cause-versus-form exchange: B argued that any omission severe enough to miseducate becomes an affirmable content defect review can catch; A answered that students infer meaning from what teachers select and omit, so political fear can produce the miseducation B fears while degrading the mechanisms that correct it—a reframing that preserved A's ranking and left B's closing rejoinder underpowered.</best_rebuttal>
